ety.text: From Middle English miracle, from Old French miracle, from Latin mīrāculum (“object of wonder”), from mīror (“to wonder at”), from mīrus (“wonderful”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)meyh₂- (“to smile, to be astonished”). Doublet of milagro and miraculum. Partially displaced native wonder, from Old English wundor (“miracle, wonder”).

senses.d: An event that appears inexplicable by the laws of nature and so is held to be supernatural in origin.
ex: Many religious beliefs are based on miracles.
An example of a miracle associated with Muhammad is the splitting of the moon.

senses.d: A fortunate outcome that prevails despite overwhelming odds against it.
An awesome and exceptional example of something.
To affect by a miracle; to work a miracle upon.
ex: Deleuze and Guattari are right in miracling fleas into the bestiary, but it is already rich enough to do without them.
They think I've miracled the dogs, as the Eucharist miracled my mother. That I, Bonne, am pulsing with holy spirit.

ety.text: From Old Galician-Portuguese miragre, a semi-learned borrowing from Latin mīrāculum (“object of wonder”). Compare Spanish milagro. Doublet of miráculo, a more recent borrowing.

ety.text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese maravilha, from Latin mīrābilia, plural of mīrābilis (“wonderful”), from mīrus (“wonderful”).

From Middle English mirour, from Old French mireor (“mirror”, literally “looker, watcher”), from mirer (“look at”), from Latin mīror (“wonder at”), from mīrus (“wonderful”), from Proto-Indo-European *smey- (“to laugh, to be glad”). Displaced native Middle English schewere, schawere, from Old English sċēawere (“mirror”, literally “watcher”), which was also the word for "spy".

senses.d: A smooth surface, usually made of glass with reflective material painted on the underside, that reflects light so as to give an image of what is in front of it.
ex: I had a look in the mirror to see if the blood had come off my face.
He broke the mirror with the pickaxe.

senses.d: An object, person, or event that reflects or gives a picture of another.
ex: His story is a mirror into the life of orphans growing up.
O goddess, heavenly bright, / Mirror of grace and majesty divine.

senses.d: A website or server that contains replicated data from another site.
ex: Although the content had been deleted from his blog, it was still found on some mirrors.

senses.d: An ethical-didactic treatise that details exemplary conduct through models, advising kings, princes, clergy, etc. on how to behave.
To reflect, as in a mirror.
To act as a reflection of, either by being identical to, or by being identical but reversed.
ex: The placement of the paintings mirrored the positions of the windows on the opposite wall.

senses.d: Of an event, activity, behavior, to be identical to; to be a copy of; to imitate closely.
ex: He tried to mirror Elvis's life by copying his fashion and mannerisms.

senses.d: To create something identical to (a website, etc.).

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French glace, from Old French glace (“ice", also "glass, mirror, radiance”), from Vulgar Latin *glacium/a, from Latin glaciēs (“ice”). The senses of "glass, mirror, radiance" were possibly derived from Frankish *glas (“glass”).
Inherited from Middle French miroir m, Old French mireor m. Equivalent to mirer + -oir.
From Vulgar Latin speclum, syncopated form of Latin speculum, from the verb speciō. Compare specolo, a borrowed doublet.

Inherited from Old Spanish espeio, from Vulgar Latin speclum (or perhaps a variant form *spiclum), syncopated form of Latin speculum. Compare the learned doublet espéculo. Cognate with English speculum, German Spiegel, Catalan espill, Portuguese espelho, and Italian specchio.
